title: Peshawar joins the kingdom
hook: the frontier city is brought into the kingdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir, and your line was the valley. Did you find a sheltered place to rest? Today we go west, to the other end of the map. Day nine hundred eighteen.

Peshawar is a market town where the plains run out. Caravans unload in its bazaars: horses, dried fruit, carpets from beyond the hills. Behind the city, the road climbs west toward Afghanistan. Traders came down that road. Armies came down it too, again and again, into the Punjab. A city that sits at the mouth of a pass like that is never just a city. It's a door. Whoever holds it decides who comes in. Today: Peshawar joins the kingdom.
screen: `A CITY AT THE MOUTH OF A PASS.` → `TRADERS AND ARMIES.` → `A DOOR, NOT JUST A CITY.`

segments.voice: First, the long approach. Peshawar didn't fall in a day. For years it sat between the Sikh kingdom and the Afghan rulers, paying tribute to Lahore at times, slipping back at others. Sikh histories tell of battles on the plains around it and of the slow pull of the city toward Lahore. Second, the general. You met him a few days ago: Hari Singh Nalwa, who held the frontier. In the way Sikh histories tell it, he was the one who brought Peshawar fully into the kingdom and then governed the region. He built forts, among them the fort at Jamrud near the pass, where he would later fall. Third, what it meant. With Peshawar held, the kingdom's edge sat at the foot of the Khyber. The door that armies had used to come down into the Punjab was now held from Lahore. Sikh tradition remembers this with pride: the road that had brought invaders now had a Sikh guard on it. Fourth, the cost of an edge. A border city is never quiet. Peshawar had its own Pashtun leaders with their own loyalties, and the Afghan rulers wanted it back. Holding it meant troops, forts and constant watch. An edge is where a kingdom stands guard and where it can be struck, both at once. A fort at the mouth of a pass, its gate facing the hills: that's the edge.
screen: `YEARS OF PULL BETWEEN TWO POWERS.` · `HARI SINGH NALWA BRINGS IT IN.` · `A SIKH GUARD ON THE INVADERS' ROAD.` · `AN EDGE IS STRONG AND EXPOSED.` · then, large: `THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes at the edges. Sit and let your breath settle. Now think of the edges of your own world: the last street you know well, the people at the far side of your circle, the subjects you avoid, the hour of the day you never see. Pick one edge. Rest your attention there for a few breaths. Don't push past it. Just notice what's on the other side, and how it feels to stand at the line. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Peshawar joins the kingdom. The city at the mouth of the Khyber, pulled toward Lahore for years and brought in under Hari Singh Nalwa. Today's word.

Your line: the edge. Today, take one small step toward an edge of your world: a new street, a new voice, a question you usually skip. Then come home and notice what you brought back. Day nine hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Peshawar in histories of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign and in the stories of Hari Singh Nalwa, the general who held the north-west frontier.

notes: No year given in the voice; Peshawar paid tribute from the 1820s and was annexed in 1834 in most histories; confirm.
'For the first time in a long while, the door … held by people from the Punjab' is a strong claim; softened from 'for the first time in centuries'; confirm or cut.
Peshawar's people described as mostly Pashtun and Muslim; confirm wording is fair.
Gurmukhi ਪਿਸ਼ੌਰ (Pishaur) vs ਪਿਸ਼ਾਵਰ (Peshawar): confirm which to show.
Day 914 covered Hari Singh Nalwa and Jamrud; this day only points back to him; confirm no overlap once 914 is written.
